← Hidden Unicode Check

How to remove hidden Unicode characters once you've found them

Finding a zero-width space or a bidi-override character is only step one. Here is what actually strips them cleanly, what silently fails to, and how to stop them coming back.

Short, isolated findings: retype the line

For a short span flagged by a scan, select the visible text around it, delete the whole span, and retype it by hand rather than editing around the gap. Because the hidden character has no visible glyph, copying the same-looking text from elsewhere in the file risks carrying the hidden character along with it — retyping guarantees a clean insertion.

A visual find-and-replace usually can't do this

A plain text editor's find box typically has nowhere to put an invisible character as the search term — there's nothing to type or paste into it that reliably represents one. This only works if the editor supports searching by Unicode codepoint or a regex character class, which most general-purpose editors don't expose directly.

The command line, once you have the codepoint

This is where a scan's output becomes directly actionable: with the exact codepoint in hand, reference it by its UTF-8 byte sequence or a Unicode escape instead of by pasting the invisible character itself.

sed -i "s/\xe2\x80\x8b//g" file.md removes every zero-width space (U+200B). Repeat per distinct codepoint a scan reports — which is exactly why a scan that lists every codepoint present, not just "something was found," is what makes this a fix rather than a guess.

Git history is a separate problem

An ordinary commit removes the character from the current file, but any earlier commit that still contains it stays in the repository's history and is fetchable by anyone who clones it. If the hidden text was sensitive, or the concern is supply-chain provenance rather than just the live file, that needs a history rewrite and force-push on top of the content fix — not the content fix alone.

Stopping it from recurring

The common entry point is a copy-paste from something external — a dependency's README, a PR description, a chat transcript. Re-scan text from an external source before trusting it, the same way you'd review a diff before merging it.

Common questions

Can I just retype the affected line?

Yes, for a short, isolated finding this is the most reliable fix: select the visible text around it, delete the whole span, and retype it by hand. Because the hidden characters have no visible glyph, copy-pasting the same-looking text from elsewhere in the same file risks carrying the hidden character along with it — retyping guarantees a clean insertion.

Will a plain text editor's find-and-replace remove them?

Only if it supports searching by Unicode codepoint or a regex character class, and you know which codepoint you're removing — which is exactly what a scan gives you. A visual find-and-replace box usually can't be given an invisible character as the search term at all, since there's nothing to type or paste into it that reliably represents one.

Does a command-line tool like sed or grep handle this safely?

Yes, once you have the exact codepoint from a scan: sed -i "s/\xe2\x80\x8b//g" removes every zero-width space (U+200B) from a file, referencing the character by its UTF-8 byte sequence or a \u escape rather than by pasting it, which sidesteps the invisibility problem entirely. Repeat per codepoint found; a scan that lists every distinct codepoint present is what makes this safe rather than a guess.

Does committing the fix to git actually remove it from history?

Not on its own. An ordinary commit removes the character from the current file, but any earlier commit that still contains it remains in the repository's history and is fetchable by anyone who clones it. If the hidden text was sensitive or the concern is supply-chain provenance, that needs a history rewrite (and force-push) on top of the content fix, not the content fix alone.

How do I stop it from happening again?

Re-scan a file after any copy-paste from an external source — a dependency's README, a PR description, a chat transcript — before trusting it, since that is the common entry point. A few editors and linters can flag specific invisible-character classes automatically; where that exists, enabling it closes the gap this tool otherwise has to catch by hand each time.

Hidden Unicode Check

Paste CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules, copilot-instructions.md, a README, a PR description, or any text and find every zero-width character, invisible Unicode tag character, and bidirectional override character hiding from a human reviewer -- while an AI coding agent reading the raw bytes still sees them.

Mechanical checks, not a security audit. This tool reports the exact codepoints below at the exact positions they occur -- it never contacts a server. A finding is something worth a human look, not a verdict, and a clean result is not a safety guarantee.

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only that a scan ran or a summary was copied. Nothing you paste or upload -- no text contents, filenames, or findings -- is ever recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    What counts as a "hidden" Unicode character here?

    Two families. Invisible characters render as no visible glyph at all — zero-width spaces and joiners, the byte-order mark, Unicode Tag characters, and similar — so a person skimming the file sees nothing unusual while a program reading the raw bytes sees and can act on them. Bidirectional-control characters don't hide a character, they can hide what order characters render in, which is the Trojan Source technique.

    Does this tool upload my file or contact a server?

    No. Pasted text stays in the textarea; an uploaded file is read locally with the browser's File API and never leaves your device. This page makes no network request of its own.

    What are Unicode Tag characters, and why does this tool decode them?

    Tag characters (U+E0000–U+E007F) are invisible and map one-for-one onto printable ASCII. Since 2024 they have been the documented payload channel for hiding an entire instruction inside a file an AI agent will read — sometimes called ASCII smuggling. Rather than just flagging that tag characters are present, this tool decodes a run of them back into the plaintext they spell out, because showing what the hidden text says is more useful than just knowing something is hidden.

    What is a bidirectional override character, and why does it matter?

    RLO/LRO and their relatives (U+202E, U+202D, and the embedding/isolate family) tell a text renderer to display characters in a different visual order than they are stored in. First published as "Trojan Source" in 2021, this can make reviewed source code or text visually read one way while a compiler, interpreter, or agent processes the actual stored order — hiding a change inside what looks like a comment or a string.

    Does a clean scan mean the file is safe?

    No. This tool only reports the exact codepoints in this list at the exact positions they occur. A clean result means none of them were found in the text you pasted — it is not a security audit, and it says nothing about a prompt-injection technique that uses only ordinary visible characters.

vs-mcp-scan.html.text:
← Hidden Unicode Check

Hidden Unicode Check vs. MCP-Scan

Related tools, different jobs. MCP-Scan connects to the MCP servers in your client configuration and judges their live tool descriptions for poisoning, shadowing, and rug pulls. This checker answers one narrower, purely mechanical question about any text you paste — does it contain a specific invisible Unicode codepoint — entirely in your browser, with nothing to install.

What each tool is for

MCP-Scan (github.com/invariantlabs-ai/mcp-scan, run with uvx mcp-scan@latest) is an open-source security scanner from Invariant Labs. Per its own documentation, it searches your MCP client configuration files for configured servers, connects to each one, retrieves its live tool descriptions, and scans them — combining local checks with a call to Invariant's own Guardrailing API — for tool poisoning attacks, prompt injection in tool descriptions, cross-origin tool-shadowing attacks, and rug pulls (a tool's description changing after you already approved it, detected via hashing). Its proxy mode can also monitor and log live MCP traffic.

This checker does one narrower thing: you paste any text — an MCP tool description, a CLAUDE.md, an AGENTS.md, a README, a PR body — and it lists every zero-width or invisible-joiner character, every Unicode Tag-character run (decoded back to the hidden ASCII message it spells out), every bidirectional-override control character, and every smuggling-pattern variation selector, each with its codepoint, name, line/column, and byte offset. It runs entirely in your browser: no install, no account, and no network call of its own.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Which MCP servers do I have configured, and does a live audit of their tool descriptions flag poisoning, shadowing, or a rug pull since I last approved them?MCP-Scan — that is its entire job, and this tool does not attempt any of it.
Does this specific piece of text I already have in hand contain a zero-width character, a hidden Tag-character message, or a bidi override?This checker — a codepoint-level list, offline, with nothing installed or connected.
I don't have uv/Python set up, or I just want to check one string before deciding whether to run a fuller audit.This checker — open the page, paste the text, done.
I want ongoing, judged monitoring of live MCP servers, including techniques beyond invisible Unicode (semantic prompt injection, tool shadowing, rug pulls).MCP-Scan — this checker's codepoint list does not attempt semantic judgement at all.

The two are complementary, not competing: MCP-Scan's own stated scope already covers prompt injection in tool descriptions generally, of which invisible Unicode is one technique. This checker is a fast, offline, independently verifiable second opinion on that one specific technique — useful with or without MCP-Scan installed, and on text that has nothing to do with MCP at all.

Scan pasted text

Common questions

Should I use this checker or MCP-Scan?

Different shapes of tool for a related but different question. MCP-Scan (uvx mcp-scan@latest, from Invariant Labs) reads your MCP client configuration, connects to each configured server, retrieves its live tool descriptions, and judges them for tool poisoning, prompt injection, cross-origin tool shadowing, and rug pulls (a tool's description changing after you approved it) — combining local checks with a call to Invariant's own Guardrailing API. This checker does one narrower, purely mechanical thing: you paste any text — a tool description, a README, a CLAUDE.md, a PR body — and it lists the exact zero-width, Unicode-Tag, bidi-override, or variation-selector codepoints in it, entirely in your browser, with no install and no network call of its own. If you want a live, judged audit of every MCP server you have configured, MCP-Scan is built for exactly that and this tool does not attempt it. If you want to check one piece of pasted text for this specific invisible-character technique with nothing to install and no data leaving your browser, this is the tool for that question.

Wouldn't MCP-Scan already catch hidden Unicode in a tool description?

Likely often, since MCP-Scan's own stated scope covers prompt injection in tool descriptions generally, and hidden Unicode is one way to carry it. What this checker adds is not broader coverage of MCP — it is a specific, verifiable, offline second opinion: given the same text, it reports the exact codepoint, name, and byte offset of every invisible character on its list, with nothing sent anywhere and no dependence on a live server connection or an external API call being reachable or trusted. That is useful on its own even outside the MCP context this comparison is framed around — the same technique appears in a pasted README, a PR description, or any other text handed to an AI agent.

Why would I need a separate checker if MCP-Scan already exists?

Two reasons. First, scope: MCP-Scan's job is auditing the MCP servers you have configured, which requires installing it and letting it connect to those servers and call Invariant's API; this tool's job is checking one piece of already-in-hand text for one specific, mechanical technique, with nothing to install and no server connection at all — useful the moment you are staring at a tool description and want a fast, local answer before deciding whether to run a fuller audit. Second, this checker is not MCP-specific: it is built to check any pasted text — a CLAUDE.md, an AGENTS.md, a README, a PR description — for the same invisible-character techniques, not only MCP tool descriptions.

Is this page affiliated with MCP-Scan or Invariant Labs?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Invariant Labs or the MCP-Scan project. MCP-Scan is an open-source security scanner, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public documentation and source repository at github.com/invariantlabs-ai/mcp-scan.

vs-reading-the-file-by-hand.html.text:
Hidden Unicode Check · comparison

Hidden Unicode Check vs. reading the file by hand

A careful reviewer genuinely catches what renders visibly wrong. This page names no company or product — reading a file before trusting it is a habit most developers already have, not a competing tool.

What a careful read catches reliably

A typo, a stray visible character, an oddly-spaced word, an obviously garbled line — anything that actually changes what appears on screen is exactly what a careful reviewer is good at noticing. This tool does not replace that kind of reading.

What a careful read cannot catch, by construction

CaseReading by handThis tool
A zero-width space, joiner, or Hangul filler characterRenders as nothing — there is no glyph to see, whether or not the character is present in the fileFlags the exact codepoint, name, and byte offset regardless of whether it draws anything
A Unicode Tag character run (U+E0000–U+E007F)Attaches invisibly to ordinary-looking visible text; the sentence you read carries no visual sign a second message is riding along with itDecodes the hidden run back to the plaintext it spells out, not just a "something is here" flag
A bidi override (RLO/LRO and the embedding/isolate family)The whole mechanism is that the renderer displays a different order than the bytes are stored in — reading the screen shows you the renderer's choice, not the stored orderReports the control character itself and its position, independent of how any particular renderer chooses to display it
A variation selector used as a smuggling channelSelectors from the Variation Selectors Supplement block render as nothing extra on their own, attached silently to a visible anchor characterFlags each selector by codepoint and position, distinct from ordinary emoji-variation use

The gap that matters most: these characters are defined to be unreadable

This isn't a case of a reviewer missing something a careful enough read could have caught. A zero-width character is defined by the Unicode Standard to draw no glyph and occupy no width; a bidi override is defined to make the rendered order disagree with the stored order. Both behave exactly as specified whether or not anyone is reviewing the file — there is no reading strategy that makes an invisible character visible, because invisibility is the character's whole job. A mechanical scan over the raw codepoints, rather than the rendered screen, is not a more careful version of reading; it's a different question asked of a different layer of the file.

When to still read the file yourself

This tool only reports the exact codepoints on its list at the exact positions they occur. It is not a security audit, it does not understand what the surrounding visible text means, and it says nothing about a prompt-injection technique built entirely from ordinary, ASCII text. Judging whether a flagged character's context is actually malicious, and everything a scan of raw codepoints cannot see, is still a job for reading the file yourself.

Common questions

What does reading a file carefully actually catch?

A reviewer catches what renders visibly wrong: a typo, a stray character, an oddly-spaced word. Those are real defects and a careful read finds them the same way it always has. This tool does not replace that kind of reading -- it looks for a different, narrower class of problem.

Why can't a careful read catch a zero-width character?

Because it renders as nothing. A zero-width space, a zero-width joiner, a Hangul filler character -- every one of them is defined by the Unicode Standard to occupy no visible width and draw no glyph. There is no way to see one by looking at rendered text in a normal editor or diff view; the file simply looks like it has no character there at all, whether or not one is present in the underlying bytes.

Why is a Unicode Tag character worse than a zero-width one?

A run of Tag characters (U+E0000-U+E007F) doesn't just hide -- it spells out an entire hidden ASCII message, one Tag codepoint per hidden character, attached invisibly to whatever visible text sits next to it. A sentence that reads as an ordinary instruction to a human reviewer can carry a second, completely different instruction in Tag characters that only a program reading the raw codepoints ever sees -- which is exactly what an AI coding agent reading a pasted file does.

Why can't a careful read catch a bidi override?

Because a bidi override (RLO/LRO and the rest of the 2021 Trojan Source family) is a control character whose entire purpose is to tell the renderer to display stored characters in a different visual order than they are stored in. Reading the screen shows you the order the renderer chose to draw, not the order the bytes are actually stored in -- which is the whole mechanism, not a rendering bug.

Does a clean scan mean the file is safe?

No. This tool only reports the exact codepoints on its list at the exact positions they occur. A clean result means none of them were found in the text pasted in -- it is not a security audit, and it says nothing about a prompt-injection technique built entirely from ordinary, visible characters.
